related_questions.question: What is the basic explanation of type 2 diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: In type 2 diabetes, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use insulin well. Too much glucose then stays in your blood, and not enough reaches your cells. The good news is that you can take steps to prevent or delay the development of type 2 diabetes.

text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by the body's inability to effectively use insulin (insulin resistance) and/or insufficient insulin production by the pancreas. This leads to elevated blood glucose levels, resulting in various metabolic disturbances and long-term complications.
snippet_highlighted_words: the body's inability to effectively use insulin (insulin resistance) and/or insufficient insulin production by the pancreas

list.title: Insulin Resistance:
list.snippet: Cells, particularly in muscle, liver, and fat tissue, become less responsive to insulin, impairing glucose uptake and utilization.

list.title: Beta Cell Dysfunction:
list.snippet: While the pancreas initially produces more insulin to compensate for resistance, over time, beta cells may become damaged or less effective at producing insulin, leading to insufficient insulin production.

list.title: Increased Liver Glucose Production:
list.snippet: The liver may produce excessive glucose, further contributing to elevated blood sugar levels.

list.title: Inflammation and Other Metabolic Abnormalities:
list.snippet: Insulin resistance and other metabolic issues can trigger inflammation and abnormalities in fat and protein metabolism, further complicating the disease.

list.title: Hyperglycemia:
list.snippet: Elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) are the hallmark of type 2 diabetes and can damage blood vessels and nerves.

list.title: Long-term Complications:
list.snippet: Damage to blood vessels and nerves can lead to various complications, including cardiovascular disease (heart attack, stroke), nerve damage (neuropathy), kidney disease (nephropathy), and vision loss (retinopathy).
Obesity and Overweight: Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, is a major risk factor.
Physical Inactivity: Lack of exercise contributes to insulin resistance.
Unhealthy Diet: Diets high in processed foods, saturated fats, and refined carbohydrates increase risk.
Age: Risk increases with age, particularly after 35.
Family History: Genetic predisposition plays a role.
Ethnicity: Certain ethnicities have a higher risk.
Other Factors: Hormonal disorders, certain medications, and sleep disturbances can also contribute.
